title: gold_quality_history.external_coverage_rate reads 158.33% — implausible, likely denominator defect in producer
description:
UNVERIFIED, TREAT AS A LEAD NOT A CONFIRMED DEFECT. task-065's implement-agent measured gold_quality_history's external_coverage_rate metric at 158.33 (i.e. 158.33%) at every recent pipeline run while querying the live model for an unrelated fix. A coverage rate over 100% is not coherent — it implies a numerator exceeding its denominator, most likely because the producer notebook computes them from mismatched row populations (e.g. a filtered numerator over an unfiltered, or differently-scoped, denominator).

This was a side observation, not a targeted measurement — re-confirm the 158.33% figure independently before diagnosing anything further, and identify which of the two candidate producer notebooks (silver_to_gold or data_quality_checks — whichever actually writes metric_name='external_coverage_rate' rows) owns the computation. files_affected above lists both candidates; narrow to the actual one before editing.

No measure in gold_quality_history.tmdl currently surfaces external_coverage_rate directly (per task-065's measurement), so there is no known user-facing symptom yet — this is purely a data-quality-observability defect until proven otherwise.

Do not commit or push without confirming with Erik first, consistent with the rest of Phase 5's out-of-spec defect tasks.
acceptanceCriteria: The 158.33% figure is independently re-measured against the live model (not taken on task-065's word), across at least the most recent 3 pipeline runs, to confirm it is a persistent pattern and not a one-off.

The producer of the external_coverage_rate metric_name row is identified with evidence (which notebook, which computation), and the numerator/denominator populations are shown to be mismatched — or shown NOT to be, in which case this closes as an honest null result (the number may be legitimate if the metric's definition genuinely allows >100%, e.g. it's a coverage ratio against a shrinking baseline).

If a defect is confirmed: the computation is fixed so the metric reads as a coherent percentage (0-100% or whatever range the metric's definition actually implies), and the fix is demonstrated against a live re-run, not just reasoned about.
If no defect is confirmed: docs/data_quality_framework.md or docs/data_quality_architecture.md records what the 158.33% actually means, so it isn't re-flagged as a mystery in a future session.
Erik's half: deploy (if a fix was made) and confirm the corrected value on a subsequent scheduled or manual run.
